current.role: Houston-based co-author on a long run of papers from Andrea Ballabio's group on TFEB, the master switch for lysosome and autophagy genes, including the work that tied TFEB to mTOR, starvation and fat metabolism
current.sub: Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine · Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute, Texas Children's Hospital (latest PubMed affiliation, 2026) · co-author with the Ballabio, Settembre and Sardiello groups (2011–2026)
story: Cells keep themselves clean with lysosomes, small acid-filled bags that break down worn-out parts, and with autophagy, the process that delivers those parts to the lysosome. In 2011 Carmine Settembre, Andrea Ballabio and colleagues, with Tuong Huynh among the co-authors, showed that one transcription factor, TFEB, switches on a whole programme of autophagy and lysosome genes when cells are starved (SET2011). In that first paper TFEB was controlled by the kinase ERK2. The 2012 follow-up (SET2012) found the link to mTORC1, the growth-control complex that sits on the lysosome surface: when nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB and keeps it out of the nucleus, so the lysosome itself reports its state to the genes that build it.

The 2013 paper (SET2013) moved into living mice. Fasting switched on the TFEB gene in liver, muscle and kidney, and TFEB then boosted its own production in a feed-forward loop. In the liver it drove fat breakdown largely through PGC-1alpha and PPARalpha, and extra liver TFEB protected mice from diet-induced obesity. The most recent paper (FER2026) used kidney-specific mouse models to separate mTORC1 activity from TFEB/TFE3 activity and found that overactive mTORC1, not TFEB/TFE3 alone, is the main driver of kidney cysts and tumours in models of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex.

PubMed lists Tuong Huynh on about a dozen TFEB, lysosome and autophagy papers with the Ballabio, Settembre or Sardiello groups between 2011 and 2026. The early papers give no affiliation for this author; a 2020 paper and the 2026 kidney paper place Huynh at the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, and the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute of Texas Children's Hospital in Houston, where Ballabio's US laboratory is based. The exact job title could not be confirmed from an official page.

story: Mariana de Araujo appears in three Atlas studies about the lysosome surface, where mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on and off. In NAP2020 (cells and mice), mTORC1 was shown to reach the transcription factor TFEB by a special route that depends on the RagC and RagD proteins, and this route drives kidney disease in Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. In PRE2021 (cells), the stress-granule proteins G3BP1 and G3BP2 were found to hold the TSC complex, a brake on mTORC1, on the lysosome. CUI2023 is a cryo-EM structure showing how two Rag-Ragulator units hand a TFEB molecule to the mTOR active site. De Araujo is a co-author in the middle of the author list on all three.

These collaborations build on de Araujo's own first-author work. In a 2017 Science paper from Innsbruck, de Araujo and colleagues solved the crystal structure of the human LAMTOR complex, also called Ragulator: five small proteins held together by LAMTOR1 that anchor the Rag GTPases to the lysosome and set their orientation for meeting mTORC1. The paper also showed which short stretches of LAMTOR1 are needed to recruit and hold the Rags. This structure is one of the reference points for how amino acid signals reach mTORC1.

De Araujo has published with Lukas Huber's group at the Medical University of Innsbruck since a 2004 study on the p14/MP1 scaffold, an earlier-known part of the same complex. The group studies how late endosomes and lysosomes organise signaling. In 2026 de Araujo was first author of a PNAS paper showing that the BORC complex, which moves lysosomes along the cell's tracks, can combine with subunits of a related complex, BLOC-1, to take on different transport jobs. story: After a heart transplant, patients take drugs for life to stop the immune system from attacking the new heart. The standard drugs, calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, can damage the kidneys, and over the years many transplanted hearts develop cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a thickening of the coronary arteries. Everolimus blocks mTOR, which slows the growth of immune cells and of the cells in artery walls. Giancarlo Maruri Munaretto was senior author of a 2026 meta-analysis in JHLT Open (VITTE2026) that pooled 60 studies with 1,786 heart transplant recipients to weigh up everolimus.

A meta-analysis combines the results of many separate studies to get a clearer overall answer. Here, everolimus-based treatment slowed the artery thickening seen on intravascular ultrasound and kept kidney function better when the dose of calcineurin inhibitors was lowered. Deaths were about the same, but side effects and stopping the drug were more common. The study draws on data from people, so it speaks directly to patient care.

PubMed lists Munaretto at the Department of Medicine of Universidade do Contestado in Concordia, Santa Catarina, Brazil, as senior author of one other 2026 meta-analysis, on sealing the needle track with saline to prevent a collapsed lung after CT-guided lung biopsy. No personal page was found to show career stage.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus in heart transplant recipients: A meta-analysis

story: Androgenetic alopecia is the common pattern hair loss driven by male hormones. A hormone called DHT shrinks hair follicles, and the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase makes DHT from testosterone. story: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells, the antibody factories of the bone marrow. A standard drug against it is bortezomib, which blocks the proteasome, the machine that destroys unwanted proteins, so that myeloma cells choke on their own protein waste. Many patients eventually stop responding. In FU2026, Cong Xu's group found that a small RNA piece cut from a transfer RNA, called tRF-17-8SPOL52, is raised in relapsed or treatment-resistant myeloma. It lowers RUBCN, a protein that normally holds back autophagy, the cell's self-digestion system. With the brake removed, autophagy speeds up and helps myeloma cells survive bortezomib. The link to mTOR is indirect: autophagy is one of the main processes mTORC1 keeps in check.

Xu works in the Department of Hematology of the Seventh Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University in Shenzhen. In 2025 Xu was senior author of a study that used the US FDA adverse event reporting database to map lung side effects, such as pneumonia and interstitial lung disease, linked to the antibody drugs approved for myeloma. No personal institutional page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

story: In worms and flies, turning down TOR signalling can stretch lifespan dramatically. In mice, rapamycin also works, but the gain is far smaller. The 2026 review led by Denisa Pirscoveanu, with Aurel Popa-Wagner as senior author, offers an explanation: in simple organisms aging runs through a few dominant pathways, whereas in mammals it emerges from many organs talking to each other, with redundant genes, hormonal feedback, gut microbes and drug-handling differences that soften the effect of any single intervention.

For readers of this Atlas the useful message is about expectations. mTOR remains a central aging pathway in mammals, but the review argues that its leverage is diluted by system-level buffering. The paper is a synthesis of published data across species, not a new experiment.

PubMed lists Popa-Wagner at both the Department of Neurology of the University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova and the Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing at University Hospital Essen. Recent papers with this group study stroke in the aging rat brain, for example how immune genes active during early brain development contribute to post-stroke damage in old male rats.

studies.title: Biological limits of lifespan extension: evidence for a shift from pathway leverage to system-level buffering across species

story: Jan Rozman is a co-author on two Atlas studies that relied on large-scale mouse phenotyping, the systematic measuring of many body functions in the same animals. EIS2016 showed that oral spermidine, a natural compound also found in food, lengthened the lives of mice, kept heart muscle from thickening and kept the heart able to relax normally between beats. The benefit disappeared in mice whose heart muscle cells lack the autophagy gene Atg5, so autophagy, the cell's self-cleaning system, was needed for the effect. The paper also included a human diet survey linking spermidine intake to lower blood pressure and fewer heart problems, but that part is observational and cannot show cause. NEF2013 gave rapamycin, the drug that blocks mTOR, to young and old mice and measured a very wide panel of body functions. Rapamycin lengthened life but changed only a few of the classic signs of ageing, so a longer life did not mean that ageing slowed down across the whole body. Both are mouse studies.

Rozman was at the German Mouse Clinic in Neuherberg, near Munich, at the time of these studies. The German Mouse Clinic at Helmholtz Munich tests mouse models in a standardised way across many organ systems; its recent papers cover heart size, movement, behaviour, metabolism and blood values. story: David Glass is a co-author of two Atlas trials from the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research that asked whether a short course of a low-dose mTOR inhibitor can help the ageing immune system. In MAN2014, older volunteers took everolimus (RAD001), a rapamycin-like drug, for six weeks before a flu shot, and their antibody response to the vaccine rose by about 20 percent; fewer of their T cells carried PD-1, a marker of exhausted immune cells. In MAN2018, a phase 2a trial in 264 older adults, six weeks of a low-dose combination of everolimus and BEZ235 (a drug that blocks PI3K and mTOR at the active site) was linked to fewer reported infections over the following year.

These trials are the main human basis for the idea of weekly low-dose rapalogs as an anti-ageing intervention. Their limits matter: a stronger vaccine response is a lab marker, not proof of fewer infections, and a later phase 3 trial of BEZ235 (RTB101) alone did not confirm a clinical benefit.

Glass's own research line is skeletal muscle. At Novartis, as senior author, Glass led a 2019 study in aged rats showing that partial inhibition of mTORC1 with a rapalog counteracted the age-related loss of muscle mass, and contributed to work on how the enzyme HDAC4 keeps muscle in balance. Since moving to Regeneron Pharmaceuticals in Tarrytown, New York, Glass has published on how common low muscle mass is among people with obesity in the USA, on a 2025 trial identifying GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A as the main brakes on muscle mass in postmenopausal women, and in 2026 on why keeping muscle matters during drug-induced weight loss.

story: Hyo J Yang is a co-author of two structure papers from Nikola Pavletich's laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center that changed how mTOR is pictured. Structural biology works out the exact 3D shape of a protein, atom by atom, which shows how it does its job and how drugs fit into it.

The 2013 paper (YAN2013) solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, the part of the protein that adds phosphate groups to its targets. It showed that the active site sits in a deep, narrow cleft, guarded by a section called the FRB domain that acts like a gatekeeper for incoming target proteins. That explained why rapamycin, which binds the FRB domain together with its partner protein FKBP12, blocks mTOR by limiting access to the cleft, and why cancer-causing mutations cluster where they do. The 2017 paper (YAN2017) used cryo-electron microscopy, which images frozen protein complexes with an electron beam, to show the whole mTORC1 complex. It showed how the small protein RHEB, which signals growth, bends mTORC1 into its active shape, and how the inhibitor PRAS40 blocks it. Both papers describe purified proteins, not cells or animals.

These two papers are the only PubMed records for Yang with Pavletich, and no other publication or institutional page could be firmly tied to this name, which is common. The affiliation shown is the one on the papers. Hyo J Yang is a different person from Haijuan Yang, first author of both papers.

story: Nadine Cybulski is a co-author of two Atlas mouse studies from Michael Hall's lab. In 2008, mice lacking raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, only in fat tissue stayed lean, resisted diet-induced obesity and burned more energy in their fat. In 2012, mice lacking rictor, the core of mTORC2, only in the liver could not switch the liver to its fed-state programme, so it kept making glucose and made less fat. Both are mouse results.

story: Kathleen Pritchard is a co-author of both main reports of BOLERO-2 in this Atlas. BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer that had kept growing despite an aromatase inhibitor, a type of hormone therapy (BAS2012, PIC2014). All the women took the hormone drug exemestane; half also took everolimus, a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex. Resistance to hormone therapy in these cancers is linked to overactive mTOR signalling, and adding everolimus more than doubled the time before the cancer grew again (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review in the first report). That result led to the approval of everolimus for this use. The final report (PIC2014) confirmed the gain in progression-free survival, but overall survival was not significantly longer: median 31.0 versus 26.6 months. The main side effect was mouth sores (stomatitis).

For the mTOR story the trial is a landmark: it was the first large test showing that blocking mTORC1 helps patients with a common cancer, and it also shows the limits, a delay in tumour growth without a clear gain in overall survival.

Pritchard's papers in PubMed tie her to medical oncology and haematology at the Sunnybrook Odette Cancer Centre and the University of Toronto, and to the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. PubMed lists close to 190 papers with her name and a Toronto affiliation, most of them on breast cancer trials and treatment outcomes. She also co-authored the 2015 analysis of which tumour gene changes predicted benefit from everolimus in BOLERO-2. Recent examples include a 2022 study of outcomes in small, node-negative HER2-positive early breast cancer and a 2024 study on routinely collecting quality-of-life questionnaires in a breast cancer clinic. Her current title could not be confirmed from an official page.

story: Ashley Thelen is a co-author of two Zoncu lab papers in this Atlas. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, when nutrients are present. CAS2017 showed that cholesterol inside the lysosome is one of these nutrient signals: the protein SLC38A9 is needed for cholesterol to switch mTORC1 on, and NPC1, which moves cholesterol out of the lysosome and is faulty in Niemann-Pick type C disease, holds the signal back. The experiments used cell lines and patient fibroblasts. LAW2019 solved the structure of the folliculin complex, FLCN with its partner FNIP2, bound to the Rag GTPases and Ragulator on the lysosome. Folliculin acts as a checkpoint that switches on one of the Rag proteins, RagC, which mTORC1 needs to be recruited. Loss of FLCN causes Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition with kidney tumours.
Together the two papers show how mTORC1 reads the state of the lysosome: what nutrients it holds, and whether the Rag switch on its surface is in the 'on' position. Both are cell and protein studies.

Thelen was first author of a 2017 Trends in Cell Biology review, written with Zoncu, on the emerging roles of the lysosome in lipid metabolism, and co-authored a 2019 Molecular Biology of the Cell paper from Schekman's lab at Berkeley on how an autophagy-specific PI3-kinase complex controls LC3 lipidation, an early step in building autophagosomes. story: Sofia Helena Vitte was first author of a 2026 meta-analysis in JHLT Open (VITTE2026) on everolimus after heart transplantation. Everolimus is a rapamycin-like drug that blocks mTOR and is used to stop the immune system from attacking a new organ. A meta-analysis pools the numbers from many studies to get a clearer answer than any one study gives. This one pooled 60 studies with 1,786 heart transplant recipients.

Everolimus-based treatment slowed cardiac allograft vasculopathy, the narrowing of the transplanted heart's arteries that limits how long the new heart lasts, to about 57 percent of the risk seen without it. When doctors also reduced calcineurin inhibitors, older drugs that damage the kidneys, kidney function was clearly better. Deaths from any cause did not change, but side effects and stopping treatment were more common. This is evidence from transplant patients, pooled across studies of different designs.

PubMed shows Vitte's earlier work at the Atherosclerosis and Vascular Biology Laboratory of the State University of Campinas, on the Brazilian Diabetes Study of people with type 2 diabetes (2022 to 2024), and later at the Department of Medicine of the Pontifícia Universidade Católica de Campinas, including other meta-analyses on exercise after Fontan heart surgery (2025) and on preventing lung collapse after CT-guided lung biopsy (2026). current.role: Fish nutrition researcher at Shanghai Ocean University who studies why carnivorous farmed fish such as largemouth bass handle dietary carbohydrate poorly and how this links to mTOR signalling in the liver
current.sub: Research Centre of Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition, Shanghai Ocean University (affiliation on PubMed papers from 2023 to 2026)
story: Jiajie Tao is the first author of TAO2026, a study in largemouth bass, a meat-eating fish that is farmed widely in China. Fish feed is cheaper when it contains more starch, but carnivorous fish cope badly with it: their livers fill up with glycogen, the stored form of sugar, much like animals with glucose intolerance. The study asked why. It found that in the bass liver the insulin-responsive mTOR/SREBP1 pathway, which normally turns extra sugar into fat, works poorly. When this route is impaired, more of the sugar ends up stored as glycogen. The work is in fish, so it tells us about how mTOR helps decide where sugar goes in the liver, not directly about people.

PubMed lists Tao at Shanghai Ocean University's Research Centre on Environmental Ecology and Fish Nutrition on about a dozen papers since 2023, most of them on carbohydrate use in largemouth bass, usually with Songlin Li as senior author. An earlier first-author paper (2023) showed that adding cultures of the gut bacterium Clostridium butyricum to a high-starch diet reduced glycogen build-up in the bass liver and raised insulin-signalling and glycolysis genes.
No official profile was found, so training and position are given only from the publication record.

studies.title: Impaired mTOR/SREBP1-Mediated Lipogenesis as a Mechanism of Hepatic Glycogen Accumulation in a Carnivorous Fish Model, Largemouth Bass (Micropterus salmoides)

current.lab_name: Burn and Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (Wuxi, China)
current.role: Wound-repair researcher at the Burn and Trauma Treatment Center in Wuxi who tests natural compounds against scarring and diabetic wound inflammation
current.sub: Burn and Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University, and Wuxi School of Medicine, Jiangnan University (2026)
story: Hypertrophic scars are thick, raised scars that form after burns or surgery when skin cells called fibroblasts lay down too much collagen. In a 2026 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology, Peng Cao and colleagues tested dihydromyricetin, a plant compound, on fibroblasts taken from such scars and on scars in the rabbit ear, a standard animal model. The compound lowered collagen I and III and the scar marker alpha-smooth muscle actin, and the rabbit scars became flatter. At the same time the activating chemical tags on AKT and mTOR, two growth-signalling proteins, fell. The authors state that this does not prove the compound works through the mTOR pathway.

Cao works at the Burn and Trauma Treatment Center of the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University and at Jiangnan University's Wuxi School of Medicine, in a group led by Guozhong Lyu that also belongs to a Ministry of Education engineering research centre for wound repair technology. In another 2026 first-author paper Cao studied alpha-mangostin, a compound from the mangosteen fruit, and found in cultured mouse immune cells that it reduced inflammation and oxidative stress caused by high glucose, a model of diabetic wounds. Earlier career details could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Dihydromyricetin attenuates fibrosis-associated features of hypertrophic scar with accompanying changes in PI3K/AKT/mTOR-related signaling.

previous_note: Common name (Cao P has 183 hits for wound/burn terms alone); only papers with the Jiangnan Burn and Trauma Center affiliation and Lyu G as senior author were used.

current.lab_name: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University (Chongqing, China)
current.role: Pharmaceutical scientist in Lei Luo's group at Southwest University in Chongqing who studies the drug pump P-glycoprotein, and first author of the study showing that oxidative stress boosts P-glycoprotein production through mTOR
current.sub: College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, Chongqing (Lei Luo group, papers 2025–2026)
story: P-glycoprotein is a pump in the cell membrane that throws drugs back out of the cell. Cancer cells that make a lot of it can resist many drugs at once. In the Atlas study JIN2026, Jin and colleagues in Lei Luo's group showed in cells that oxidative stress (a build-up of reactive oxygen molecules) switches on a chain of signals, PI3K to AKT to mTORC1 to the RNA-unwinding protein eIF4A, that makes the cell translate more P-glycoprotein from its existing messenger RNA. Because this skips the slower step of making new RNA, it is a fast route to drug resistance.
For the Atlas, the study is an example of mTORC1 acting through eIF4A to pick which proteins get made. It was done in cultured cells; whether it happens in tumours in patients is not shown.

On PubMed, Jin works with Luo at the College of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Southwest University, on how drugs are absorbed and pumped out of cells. Earlier papers in the group include a 2025 study showing that glucosamine directly switches on intestinal P-glycoprotein and reduces drug absorption, and a 2026 study on making the colorectal cancer drug trifluridine better absorbed when taken by mouth. Career stage could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Redox-sensitive mTOR-eIF4A signaling promotes selective P-glycoprotein translation.

previous_note: Very common name; identity tied by Southwest University plus co-author Lei Luo. Not the Emory geneticist Peng Jin; do not merge.

current.lab_name: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University (Tianjin, China)
current.role: Cardiologist in Tianjin and Cangzhou who studied how a long non-coding RNA drives necroptotic heart-cell death after a blocked artery is reopened
current.sub: Department of Cardiology, Tianjin Medical University · Department of Cardiology, Cangzhou People's Hospital, Hebei (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Yanhong Su is first author of the Atlas study SU2026, with cardiologist Jun Zhang as senior author. When a blocked heart artery is reopened, the returning blood itself causes extra damage, called ischemia-reperfusion injury. Part of that damage comes from necroptosis, a programmed form of cell death in which the cell bursts. The team looked at DLX6-AS1, a long non-coding RNA, which is an RNA molecule that regulates genes without making a protein.

In mice with ischemia-reperfusion injury, DLX6-AS1 levels rose together with the necroptosis markers RIP1, RIP3 and MLKL. In rat heart cells starved of oxygen and then re-oxygenated, extra DLX6-AS1 raised the active forms of PI3K, AKT and mTOR and made necroptosis worse, while blocking DLX6-AS1 reduced cell death. Here the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway sits on the harmful side, the opposite of many heart studies in which AKT signalling protects heart cells. The work is in mice and a rat cell line.

PubMed lists Su at the cardiology departments of Tianjin Medical University and Cangzhou People's Hospital in Hebei province. No other papers or official page could be tied to this person with confidence, so the profile rests on this study.

studies.title: LncRNA DLX6-AS1 promotes necroptosis through PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway in myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury mice

previous_note: Only one paper could be tied to this person; current position not confirmed.

current.lab_name: Laboratory of Molecular Studies and Experimental Therapy, Department of Genetics, Federal University of Pernambuco (Recife, Brazil)
current.role: Researcher in Antonio Carlos de Freitas's laboratory at the Federal University of Pernambuco who studies whether human papillomavirus (HPV) is active in breast tumours
current.sub: Laboratory of Molecular Studies and Experimental Therapy, Department of Genetics, Federal University of Pernambuco (papers 2024–2026, at the time of the study)
story: HPV, the virus that causes most cervical cancers, carries three cancer-promoting genes called E5, E6 and E7. A question still under debate is whether the virus also plays a part in some breast cancers. In DEOLIVEIRA2026, Beatriz Eda de Oliveira Isídio and colleagues in Recife measured these viral genes and the RNA messages of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway in breast tumour samples. Of 92 patients, 48 had usable RNA. Tumours expressing HPV16 genes had higher PI3K and lower mTOR transcript levels. The design only shows an association between two sets of RNA measurements in tissue, so it does not prove that the virus switches the mTOR pathway on or off.

The work continues a line from the same laboratory, led by Antonio Carlos de Freitas in the Department of Genetics at the Federal University of Pernambuco. In a 2024 study of 56 patients from northeastern Brazil, on which de Oliveira Isídio was a co-author, the group detected HPV in about a third of breast tumours, mostly HPV16, often with high viral load and active E5. No institutional profile was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

studies.title: Transcriptional modulation of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway mediated by HPV16 E5, E6, and E7 oncogene expression in breast cancer.

current.lab_name: Cate Lab, Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
current.role: Researcher in Jamie Cate's lab at UC Berkeley who used ribosome profiling to show that exhausted human T cells shut down a key class of growth-related mRNAs even while mTOR is active
current.sub: Department of Molecular and Cell Biology and Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley (Cate lab, papers 2025–2026)
story: Erica Pledger was first author of a 2026 RNA Biology paper in this Atlas (PLEDGER2026), first posted as a preprint in 2025. CD8+ T cells are the immune cells that kill infected and cancer cells. When they are stimulated for too long, for example inside a tumour, they become exhausted and stop working well. The team made human CD8+ T cells exhausted in the dish and used ribosome profiling, a method that shows which messenger RNAs are actually being read by ribosomes, to see what proteins the cells were making.

One group of messages stood out: 5' TOP mRNAs, which code for ribosome parts and other protein-making machinery. Their translation is normally switched on by mTORC1, the growth-control complex. In exhausted T cells these messages were strongly held back even though mTOR activity was high, which points to a second layer of control that overrides or bypasses mTOR. The work was done in cultured human cells, not in patients.

Pledger works in Jamie Cate's lab at UC Berkeley, which studies how ribosomes and the initiation factor eIF3 decide which mRNAs are made into protein. PubMed lists two papers with Pledger's name, the preprint and the published version.

studies.title: Translational repression of 5' TOP mRNAs in chronically activated CD8+ T cells in vitro.

previous_note: Career stage not confirmed.

current.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
current.role: Researcher in the orthopedics department of Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 review on mTORC2 and its partner RICTOR in immune cells and inflammatory disease
current.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Most writing on mTOR is about mTORC1, the complex that drives growth. Jingting Xu's 2026 review in Inflammation Research, with Fengjing Guo as senior author, collects what is known about the second complex, mTORC2, and its defining partner RICTOR in the immune system. mTORC2 acts through the kinases AKT, SGK1 and PKC.

The review describes how mTORC2 shapes the choice between Th1 and Th2 helper T cells, keeps regulatory T cells stable, helps memory T cells form, and affects B-cell receptor signalling, plasma cell survival, and the behaviour of macrophages, dendritic cells and natural killer cells. In tissues its effect depends on context: it worsens inflammation in osteoarthritis and pancreatitis but restrains pro-inflammatory macrophages in colorectal cancer. Drugs that block both mTOR complexes, such as AZD2014, show early but complicated promise. The paper is a review of published work, not new data.

PubMed lists Jingting Xu at the Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Because the name is common, no wider publication record is attributed here.

studies.title: The role of mTORC2/RICTOR in immune cells and inflammatory diseases.

previous_note: Common name; no career details beyond the Atlas paper.

current.lab_name: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (Hohhot, China)
current.role: Radiation oncology researcher in Hohhot and first author of a study linking the PIK3CA E545K mutation to faster growth and invasion of cervical cancer through AKT/mTOR signalling
current.sub: Department of Radiation Oncology, The Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: PIK3CA is the gene for the catalytic part of PI3K, an enzyme at the top of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR growth pathway. Certain spelling mistakes in this gene, called hotspot mutations, keep the enzyme switched on. In the Atlas study HUANG2026 in Molecular Genetics and Genomics, Congxiu Huang was first author. The team sequenced tumours from 61 patients with cervical cancer and found PIK3CA among the most often mutated genes. They then put the E545K mutation, one of the common hotspots, into cervical cancer cell lines. The cells grew and invaded faster, died less, and showed stronger AKT/mTOR signalling. Human cancer cells grown as tumours in mice (a xenograft model) behaved the same way. The work suggests that patients whose tumours carry this mutation might be candidates for drugs against the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, but it did not test such drugs in patients.

PubMed lists Huang at the Department of Radiation Oncology of the Affiliated Hospital of Inner Mongolia Medical University in Hohhot, with Sun X as senior author. Because the name is common, no other paper could be tied to this person with confidence, and no official profile page was found.

studies.title: Recurrent PIK3CA-E545K mutation promotes cervical cancer growth and invasion via AKT/mTOR signaling.

current.lab_name: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (Singapore)
current.role: First author of the first systematic review of rapamycin and related drugs given to people for ageing, from the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program at the National University of Singapore
current.sub: Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program, Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (at the time of the study, 2024)
story: Deborah J W Lee was first author of a 2024 systematic review in The Lancet Healthy Longevity (LEE2024). A systematic review gathers every study that meets fixed rules and judges them together, which makes it stronger than any single trial. The team screened about 18,400 records and kept 19 studies in which people took rapamycin or a related drug (a rapalog) with ageing-related outcomes in mind. The authors describe it as the first systematic review of its kind.

The picture was mixed. Measures of the immune system, the heart and blood vessels, and the skin improved in some studies. Hormone, muscle and brain measures showed no clear change. Healthy people had no serious side effects, but people who already had age-related diseases had more infections and higher cholesterol and triglycerides. For the Atlas this is one of the strongest summaries of what rapamycin does in humans, and it also shows how few human studies there are.

The paper lists Lee at the Healthy Longevity Translational Research Program of the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore. No other publication could be tied to this author with confidence, and a current position could not be confirmed.

studies.title: Targeting ageing with rapamycin and its derivatives in humans: a systematic review

previous_note: A Deborah J W Lee at Changi General Hospital, Department of Laboratory Medicine (2023, PMID 37627966, co-author Tar-Choon Aw also NUS) may be the same person, but common surname and no shared co-author, so left out.
